'''''Taraxacum officinale''''', the '''dandelion''' or '''common dandelion''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TAOF|taxon=Taraxacum officinale|access-date=8 December 2015}}</ref> is a herbaceous [[perennial]] flowering plant in the daisy family, [[Asteraceae]]. The common dandelion is well-known for its yellow [[flower head]]s that turn into round balls of many [[Pappus (botany)|silver-tufted]] fruit, which [[Wind dispersal|disperse in the wind]]. These balls are sometimes called "clocks" or "blowballs".

Originally native to [[Eurasia]], as a result of its hardiness and easy propagation, the dandelion has become widely established across several continents. It has been introduced to southern Africa, the Americas, Australia, and New Zealand. It grows in [[temperate regions]] of the world in areas with moist soils. They are able to grow in a variety of environments and are tolerant of crowding, extreme temperatures, and low moisture.

The dandelion is often considered a [[weed]], especially in lawns, but it is increasingly being recognised in its native regions as useful for attracting birds and pollinating insects. In one study, it ranked as the fourth most important source of pollen. Although dandelion pollen is considered to be an early food resource for some emerging pollinators in spring, it has also been found to lack certain essential nutrients and can lead to declining brood health for bees.<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Vanderplanck |first1= M. |last2= Gilles |first2= H. |last3= Nonclercq |first3= D. |last4= Duez |first4= P. |last5= Gerbaux |first5= P. |title= Asteraceae Paradox: Chemical and Mechanical Protection of Taraxacum Pollen |journal= Insects|date= 2020 |volume= 11 |issue= 5 |page= 304 |doi= 10.3390/insects11050304 |doi-access= free |pmid= 32422920 |pmc= 7290674 }}</ref>
The leaves, flowers, and roots are sometimes used as food and in [[Medical herb|herbal medicine]].

==Description==
[[File:Two stages in the life cycle of a dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) – flower head and seed head.jpg|thumb|left|Two life cycle stages of ''Taraxacum officinale'': flower head (left) and seed head (right)|alt=Two stages in the life of a common dandelion: flower head and seed head]]
''Taraxacum officinale'' grows from a (generally unbranched) [[taproot]] and produces several hollow, leafless flower stems,<ref name="Rose-2006">{{cite book |first=Francis |last=Rose |title=The wild flower key |date=2006 |publisher=Penguim BooksLtd. |location=London |isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0 }}</ref>{{rp|470}} typically {{convert|5-40|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} tall, but occasionally reaching up to {{convert|70|cm|abbr=on}} tall. The stems can be tinted purplish, are upright or lax, and produce [[flower head]]s that are held as tall or taller than the foliage. The foliage may be upright-growing or horizontally spreading; the leaves have petioles that are either unwinged or narrowly winged. The stems can be [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] or sparsely covered with short hairs. Plants have milky [[latex]], and the leaves are all [[Basal leaf|basal]]; each flowering stem lacks [[bract]]s and has one single flower head. The yellow flower heads lack receptacle bracts, and all the flowers, which are called [[floret]]s, are ligulate and bisexual. In many lineages, the seeds are mostly produced by [[apomixis]],<ref name="Morley-1969" /> even though the flowers are frequently visited by diverse insects.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| pmid = 25754608| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| volume = 18| issue = 1| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

The leaves are {{convert|5-45|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|1-10|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide, and they are oblanceolate, oblong, or obovate in shape, with the bases gradually narrowing to the petiole. The leaf margins are typically shallowly lobed to deeply lobed and often lacerate or toothed with sharp or dull teeth.<ref name="Morley-1969" />

The calyculi (the cuplike bracts that hold the florets) are composed of 12 to 18 segments; each segment is reflexed and sometimes glaucous. The lanceolate-shaped bractlets are arranged in two series, with acuminate apices. The {{convert|14-25|mm|frac=4}} wide involucres are green to dark green or brownish-green, with dark grey or purplish tips. The florets number 40 to over 100 per head, having yellow or orange-yellow corollas.

The fruit, called [[cypselae]],<ref name="New York Botanical Garden">{{cite web|url=http://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/glossary/glossary-details/?irn=1883|title=Cypsela|publisher=Steere Herbarium, New York Botanical Garden|access-date=18 February 2020}}</ref> range in colour from olive-green or olive-brown to straw-coloured or greyish; they are oblanceoloid in shape and {{convert|2-3|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} long, with slender beaks. The fruit have 4 to 12 ribs that have sharp edges. The silky [[Pappus (botany)|pappi]], which form the parachutes, are white to silver-white in colour and around 6 mm wide. Plants typically have 24 or 40 pairs of chromosomes, while some have 16 or 32 pairs.<ref name="Efloras-2" />

==Taxonomy==

[[Carl Linnaeus]] named the species ''[[Leontodon]] taraxacum'' in 1753. The current genus name ''Taraxacum'' derives possibly from the [[Arabic]] ''Tharakhchakon'',<ref name="Morley-1969" /> or from the [[Greek language|Greek]] ''Tarraxos''.<ref name="Kowalchik-1987" /> The specific name ''officinalis'' refers to its value as a medicinal [[herb]], and is derived from the word ''opificina'', later ''officina'', meaning a workshop or pharmacy.<ref name="Stearn-1992" />

The taxonomy of the genus ''[[Taraxacum]]'' is complicated by [[apomictic]] and [[polyploid]] lineages,<ref name="Wittzell-1999" /><ref name="Dijk-2003" /> and the taxonomy and nomenclatural situation of ''T. officinale'' is not yet fully resolved.<ref name="Efloras-2" /> The taxonomy of this genus has been complicated by the recognition of numerous species,<ref name="Tutin-1976" /> [[subspecies]] and [[microspecies]]. For example, the UK flora currently includes 239 species (of which 58 [[endemism|endemic]] and 45 non-native),<ref name="PlantAtlas-2020">{{cite web | title=Dandelion ''Taraxacum'' F.H.Wigg. | website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.fsn |access-date=2025-03-21}}</ref> and Rothmaler's ''Flora of Germany'' accepts roughly 70 microspecies.<ref name="Rothmaler-1966" />

''T. officinale'' has a fossil record that goes back to [[glacial]] and [[interglacial]] times in Europe.<ref>{{cite web |title=Taraxacum officinale complex (dandelion) |date=2019 |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/52773 |access-date=2019-06-17 |publisher=Cabi.org |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.52773 }}</ref>

===European dandelions===
''Taraxacum officinale L''. (dandelion) is a vigorous weed in Europe with diploid sexual populations in the southern regions and partially overlapping populations of diploid sexuals and triploid or tetraploid apomicts in the central and northern regions.

[[File:Taraxacum officinale PID1200-1.jpg|thumb|Dandelion in [[Toško Čelo]], Slovenia]]

These European dandelions can be divided into two groups. The first group reproduces sexually, as do most seed plants. This group consists of dandelions that have a diploid set of chromosomes, and are sexually self-incompatible. Sexual reproduction involves a reduction of the somatic chromosome number by meiosis followed by a restoration of the somatic chromosome number by fertilisation. Diploid dandelions have eight pairs of chromosomes, and meiosis is regular with normal pairing of homologous chromosomes at the metaphase I stage of meiosis.<ref name="van Baarlen-2000">{{cite journal |vauthors=van Baarlen P, van Dijk PJ, Hoekstra RF, de Jong JH |title=Meiotic recombination in sexual diploid and apomictic triploid dandelions (Taraxacum officinale L.) |journal=Genome |volume=43 |issue=5 |pages=827–35 | date=October 2000 |pmid=11081973 |doi= 10.1139/g00-047 |bibcode=2000Genom..43..827B }}</ref>

The second group consists of polyploid (mostly triploid) apomicts, meaning that both a viable embryo as well as a functional endosperm is formed without prior fertilisation. In contrast to the sexual diploids, the pairing of chromosomes at metaphase I in triploid apomicts is strongly reduced. However pairing is still sufficient to allow some recombination between homologous chromosomes.<ref name="van Baarlen-2000" />

===North American dandelions===
[[File:Taraxacum officinale 039.jpg|thumb|[[Saint-Prosper-de-Champlain, Quebec]], Canada]]

The plants introduced to North America, originally as a food crop, are triploids that mainly reproduce by obligate gametophytic apomixis<ref name="Efloras-2" /><ref name="Lyman-1984" /> Though sexual dandelion plants are known in North America, almost all are clones that produce genetically identical seeds through apomixis.<ref name="McPeek-2007">{{cite journal |last1=McPeek |first1=Tamara M. |last2=Wang |first2=Xianzhong |title=Reproduction of Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) in a Higher CO2 Environment |journal=Weed Science |date=2007 |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=334–340|doi=10.1614/WS-07-021 |bibcode=2007WeedS..55..334M |s2cid=86250272 }}</ref> Some authorities recognise two subspecies of ''Taraxacum officinale'', including:<ref name="Barnes-2007" />

* ''Taraxacum officinale'' subsp. ''officinale'', which is commonly called common dandelion or wandering dandelion.
* ''Taraxacum officinale'' subsp. ''vulgare'' (Lam.) Schinz & R. Keller, which is commonly called common dandelion.

A third taxon sometimes formerly considered a subspecies ''Taraxacum officinale'' subsp. ''ceratophorum'' (Ledeb.) Schinz ex Thellung, is now generally treated as a separate species, ''[[Taraxacum ceratophorum]]''.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Taraxacum ceratophorum (Ledeb.) DC. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=1935-01-01 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:253012-1 | access-date=2025-03-21}}</ref><ref name="Calflora" /><ref name="Efloras" /> It has a [[Holarctic realm|holarctic]] distribution.<ref name="POWO"/>

===Etymology===
[[File:Nottuln, Bauerschaft Stevern -- 2020 -- 7049.jpg|thumb|"Clocks" or "blowballs" above the grass]]

The Latin name ''Taraxacum'' derives from the [[Arabic]] {{lang|ar-Latn|tarakhshaqūn}}, meaning "bitter herb".<ref name="Gledhill-2008">Gledhill, David (2008). ''The Names of Plants''. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback). pp 279, 371</ref> The Arabic term is possibly of [[Persian language|Persian]] origin.<ref>{{cite dictionary |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/taraxacum |dictionary=Collins |title=Taraxacum |access-date=2 May 2025}}</ref> Persian polymath [[Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi|Al-Razi]] used the word {{lang|ar-Latn|tarakhshaqūn}} in relation to dandelions, chicory, and endives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Neves |first1=Liz |title=Northeast Medicinal Plants: Identify, Harvest, and Use 111 Wild Herbs for Health and Wellness |date=2 June 2020 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-1-60469-913-5 |page=14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=femvDwAAQBAJ |language=en}}</ref> Al-Razi wrote "the {{lang|ar-Latn|tarakhshaqūn}} is like chicory, but more efficacious"; it is unclear exactly to which plant Al-Razi referred however.<ref name="Skeat-1888" /> If Persian in origin, the word could have originally meant "bitter [[purslane]]" from ''تلک'' (''talk'' or bitter) and ''چکش'' (''chakūk'' or purslane).<ref>{{cite book |title=The Australian Oxford dictionary |date=2005 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=South Melbourne, Vic |isbn=978-0-19-173505-9 |edition=2nd |section=Taraxacum}}</ref> [[Gerard of Cremona]], in translating Arabic to Latin around 1170, spelled it ''tarasacon''.<ref name="Skeat-1888">Reported in ''An Etymological Dictionary of the English Language'', by Walter W. Skeat (1888) ([https://archive.org/details/etymologicaldict00skeauoft Downloadable at Archive.org]). In ''An Etymology Dictionary of Modern English'' by Ernest Weekley (1921) it is reported that Arabic طرشقون‎ ''tarashaqun'' is derivable in turn from Persian تلخ چکوک ''talkh chakok'', bitter herb ([https://archive.org/details/etymologicaldict00weekuoft Downloadable at Archive.org]).</ref>

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''officinale'' refers to the [[Latin]] word for 'medicinal' or 'of the apothecaries'.<ref>{{cite book |last=Coombes |first=Allen |title=The A to Z of Plant Names: A Quick Reference Guide to 4000 Garden Plants |publisher=Timber Press |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-60469-196-2 |location=Portland, OR, US |page=40}}</ref>

''T. officinale'' has many English common names (some of which are no longer in use), lion's-tooth, cankerwort, milk-witch, yellow-gowan, Irish daisy, monks-head, priest's-crown and puff-ball;<ref name="Britton-1970" /> other common names include, faceclock, pee-a-bed, wet-a-bed,<ref name="Nps.gov-2018" /> swine's snout,<ref name="Loewer-2001" /> white endive, and wild endive.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dandelion clock |url=http://medical-dictionary.thefreedictionary.com/Dandelion+clock |work=TheFreeDictionary.com}}</ref> The balls of seed heads are called "clocks" in both British and American English<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/blowball|title=Definition of "blowball" - Collins English Dictionary|work=collinsdictionary.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://dictionary.infoplease.com/blowball|title=blowball: meaning and definitions|work=infoplease.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ldoceonline.com/dictionary/dandelion-clock |title=dandelion clock - Definition from Longman English Dictionary Online |publisher=Ldoceonline.com |access-date=2010-07-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://americanheritage.yourdictionary.com/clock|title=Clock dictionary definition - clock defined|work=yourdictionary.com|access-date=2013-01-25|archive-date=2016-01-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160120075828/http://americanheritage.yourdictionary.com/clock}}</ref> or "blowballs".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://encyclopedia2.thefreedictionary.com/blowball|title=blowball|work=TheFreeDictionary.com}}</ref>

The common name ''dandelion'' comes from the [[French language|French]] ''dent de lion'', or "lion's tooth", in reference to the plant's jagged-edged leaves.<ref name="Kowalchik-1987" />  "Pee-a-bed" and "wet-a-bed" reflect the modern French term for the plant, ''pissenlit''. This name and all those that imply ramped-up urine production refer to its well-known [[diuretic]] properties.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=The Diuretic Effect in Human Subjects of an Extract of Taraxacum officinale Folium over a Single Day |year=2009 |pmc=3155102 |last1=Clare |first1=B. A. |last2=Conroy |first2=R. S. |last3=Spelman |first3=K. |journal=Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine |volume=15 |issue=8 |pages=929–934 |doi=10.1089/acm.2008.0152 |pmid=19678785 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:WeilerVlbg7.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|A field covered in blooming dandelions and [[Bellis perennis|daisies]] in [[Weiler, Austria]]]]

''Taraxacum officinale'' is native to Europe and Asia,<ref>{{cite book|author1=Vít Bojňanský|author2=Agáta Fargašová|title=Atlas of Seeds and Fruits of Central and East-European Flora: The Carpathian Mountains Region|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QSMe0qHGVaAC&pg=PA751|access-date=29 October 2010|year=2007|publisher=シュプリンガー・ジャパン株式会社|isbn=978-1-4020-5361-0|pages=751–}}</ref> and was originally imported to America as a food crop.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Tekiela|first1=Stan|title=Wildflowers of Minnesota: Field Guide|date=1999|publisher=Adventure Publications, Inc.|location=Cambridge, Minnesota|isbn=978-1-885061-63-8|page=343}}</ref> It is now [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] throughout North America (including all 50 states of the US and most Canadian provinces),<ref name="Alaska Naturall Heritage-2010" /> southern Africa, South America, New Zealand, Australia, and India.

The plant grows in [[temperate regions]] of the world in [[lawn]]s, on roadsides, disturbed banks, shores of waterways, and other areas with moist soils.
They are very hardy plants, able to grow in a variety of environments, and are tolerant of crowding, extremes of temperature, and low moisture.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dandelion, Taraxacum officinale |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/dandelion-taraxacum-officinale/ |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |language=en-US}}</ref>

The plant is coveted by collectors in regions where the plant is trickier to grow such as the tropics, where people would often resort to smuggling seeds from overseas.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wong |first=James |author-link=James Wong (ethnobotanist) |date=16 May 2021 |title=Why the dandelion blows away some plant collectors |language=en |newspaper=The Guardian |url=http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2021/may/16/the-dandelion-blows-away-collectors |access-date=9 September 2021}}</ref>

===Conservation===
''Taraxacum officinale'' was evaluated in 2013 by the [[IUCN]] as "Least Concern" due to a large and stable population.<ref name="Khela-2013" /> It was similarly evaluated by [[NatureServe]] in 2016 as "Globally Secure", G5.<ref name="NatureServe-2023">{{cite web |last1=NatureServe |title=''Taraxacum officinale'' |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.135912/Taraxacum_officinale |website=NatureServe Explorer |access-date=28 October 2023 |location=Arlington, Virginia |date=2023 |archive-date=28 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230528085148/https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.135912/Taraxacum_officinale |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Bombus ruderarius - Taraxacum officinale - Keila.jpg|thumb|Dandelions provide both pollen and nectar for insects.]]

It is considered a [[noxious weed]] in some jurisdictions,<ref name="Stewart-Wade-2002">{{cite journal |last=Stewart-Wade |first=S. M. |author-link=Sally Stewart-Wade |author2=S. Newmann |author3=L.L.Collins |author4=G.J. Boland |year=2002 |title=The biology of Canadian weeds. 117. ''Taraxacum officinale'' G.H. Weber ex Wiggers |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=825–853 |doi=10.4141/P01-010 |doi-access=}}</ref> and is considered to be a nuisance in residential and recreational lawns in North America.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Richardson|first=Jonathan|title=In praise of the archenemy|journal=Audubon|year=1985|volume=87|pages=37–39}}</ref> It is also an important weed in agriculture and causes significant economic damage because of its infestation in many crops worldwide.<ref name="Stewart-Wade-2002" />

''T. officinale'' can serve as an [[Bioindicator|indicator plant]] for soil [[potassium]] and [[calcium]], as the plant favours soils with relatively low concentrations of calcium, but favours soils with relatively high concentrations of potassium.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.almanac.com/news/gardening/gardening-advice/weeds-indicator-plants|title=Weeds as Indicator Plants|last=Almanac|first=Old Farmer's|website=Old Farmer's Almanac|language=en|access-date=2020-04-10}}</ref>

The dandelion is a common colonist of disturbed habitats, both from wind blown seeds and seed germination from the seed bank.<ref name="Fs.fed.us" /> The seeds remain viable in the seed bank for many years, with one study showing germination after nine years. This species is a somewhat prolific seed producer, with 54 to 172 seeds produced per head, and a single plant can produce more than 5,000 seeds a year. It is estimated that more than 97,000,000 seeds/[[hectare]] could be produced yearly by a dense stand of dandelions.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Binning|first1=Kim|title=Dandelion|url=https://fyi.uwex.edu/weedsci/2002/11/12/dandelion/|website=University of Wisconsin Weed Science Cooperative Extension|date=2002}}</ref> When released, the seeds can be spread by the wind up to several hundred meters from their source. The seeds are also a common contaminant in crop and forage seeds. The plants are adaptable to most soils and the seeds are not dependent on cold temperatures before they will germinate but they need to be within the top {{convert|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on|0}} of soil.<ref name="Alaska Naturall Heritage-2010" /> Dandelions can also regenerate themselves from fragments of taproot.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martinkova |first1=Zdenka |last2=Honek |first2=Alois |last3=Pekar |first3=Stano |title=The Role of Nurse Plants in Facilitating the Germination of Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) Seeds |journal=Weed Science |date=2014 |volume=62 |issue=3|pages=474–482 |doi=10.1614/WS-D-13-00162.1 |bibcode=2014WeedS..62..474M |s2cid=85658841 }}</ref>

''T. officinale'' is food for the [[caterpillar]]s of several [[Lepidoptera]] (butterflies and moths), such as the [[tortrix moth]] ''[[Celypha rufana]]''. See also List of Lepidoptera that feed on dandelions.

Even though dandelion pollen is of poor nutritional quality for [[honey bee]]s, they readily consume it, and it can be an important source of nutritional diversity in heavily managed monocultures such as that of blueberries,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schmidt|first1=Justin O.|last2=Thoenes|first2=Steven C.|last3=Levin|first3=M.D.|title=Survival of honey bees, Apis mellifera (Hymenoptera: Apidae), fed various pollen sources|journal=Annals of the Entomological Society of America|date=1987|volume=80|issue=2|pages=176–183|doi=10.1093/aesa/80.2.176}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Girard|first1=Mélissa|last2=Chagnon|first2=Madeleine|last3=Fournier|first3=Valérie|title=Pollen diversity collected by honey bees in the vicinity of Vaccinium spp. crops and its importance for colony development|journal=Botany|date=2012|volume=90|issue=7|pages=545–555|doi=10.1139/b2012-049|bibcode=2012Botan..90..545G |hdl=20.500.11794/39125|hdl-access=free}}</ref> or in early spring, as one of the first flowers to bloom.<ref>{{cite web |first=Madison |last=Dapcevich |url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/bees-dandelions-food/ |title=Bees Need Dandelions for Food in the Spring? |date=22 March 2024 |work=[[Snopes]] |access-date=13 January 2025 }}</ref> Honey bees have not been shown to lower their pollination activity on nearby fruit crops when foraging on dandelions.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Laverty|first1=Terence|last2=Hiemstra|first2=Henry|title=Effects of flowering dandelions as a competitor to flowers of fruit trees for pollen-collecting honey bees in Ontario|journal=The Proceedings of the Entomological Society of Ontario|date=1998|volume=129|pages=3–8 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/139964#page/279/mode/1up }}</ref>

While not in bloom, this species is sometimes confused with others, such as ''[[Chondrilla juncea]]'', that have similar [[basal rosette]]s of foliage.<ref name="Stewart-Wade-2002" /> Another plant, sometimes referred to as [[Leontodon autumnalis|fall dandelion]], is very similar to dandelion, but produces "yellow fields" later. Its blooms resemble some of the species of ''[[Sonchus]]'', but are larger.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/sonchus/ |title=Sonchus |work=North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox }}</ref>

The dandelion thrives in conditions of elevated carbon dioxide, growing to a higher biomass and producing a larger number of viable seeds. Therefore, it is anticipated that the dandelion will become more competitive and widespread as atmospheric carbon dioxide levels increase.<ref name="McPeek-2007"/>

It is increasingly being recognised in its native regions as an excellent wildflower for attracting pollinating insects and birds that feed on the seeds.<ref name="Wildlife Trusts">{{cite web | title=Common dandelion | website=The Wildlife Trusts | url=https://www.wildlifetrusts.org/wildlife-explorer/wildflowers/common-dandelion | access-date=2025-03-21}}</ref><ref name="RHS-2025">{{cite web | title=Dandelion / RHS | website=RHS | date=2025-02-04 | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/weeds/dandelion | access-date=2025-03-21}}</ref><ref name="RHS2-2025">{{cite web | title=Taraxacum officinale | website=Herbaceous Perennial/RHS | date=2025-03-20 | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/232327/taraxacum-officinale/details | access-date=2025-03-21}}</ref> In one study, it ranked as the fourth most important pollen source, after [[Salix|willow]], [[Filipendula ulmaria|meadowsweet]] and [[Rubus fruticosus|blackberry]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Wright | first1=Ellen K. | last2=Timberlake | first2=Thomas P. | last3=Baude | first3=Mathilde | last4=Vaughan | first4=Ian P. | last5=Memmott | first5=Jane | title=Quantifying the production of plant pollen at the farm scale | journal=New Phytologist | volume=242 | issue=6 | date=2024 | issn=0028-646X | doi=10.1111/nph.19763 | doi-access=free | pages=2888–2899 | pmid=38622779 | bibcode=2024NewPh.242.2888W }}</ref>

===Culinary===
The plant has several [[culinary]] uses: the flowers are used to make [[Dandelion wine (wine)|dandelion wine]],<ref name="Cooks.com" /> the greens are used in salads, the roots have been used to make a coffee substitute (when baked and ground into powder) and the plant was used by [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]]s as a food and medicine.<ref>{{Cite book | author=Clarke, Charlotte Bringle | title=Edible and useful plants of California | year=1977 | publisher=University of California Press | location=Berkeley | isbn=978-0-520-03261-3 | page=191}}</ref>

Dandelions are harvested from the wild or grown on a small scale as a [[leaf vegetable]]. The leaves (called dandelion greens) can be eaten cooked or raw in various forms, such as in [[soup]] or [[salad]]. They are probably closest in character to [[Mustard plant|mustard]] greens. Usually the young leaves and unopened buds are eaten raw in salads, while older leaves are cooked. Raw leaves have a slightly bitter taste. Dandelion salad is often accompanied with hard-boiled [[egg (food)|egg]]s. The leaves are high in [[Vitamin A|vitamins A]] and [[vitamin C|C]], as well as [[iron]], [[phosphorus]], and [[potassium]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Benoliel|first=Doug|title=Northwest Foraging: The Classic Guide to Edible Plants of the Pacific Northwest|publisher=Skipstone|year=2011|isbn=978-1-59485-366-1|edition=Rev. and updated|location=Seattle, WA|page=73|oclc=668195076}}</ref>

Dandelion flowers can be used to make dandelion [[wine]], for which there are many recipes.<ref name="Winemaking-2004" /> Most of these are more accurately described as "dandelion-flavoured wine", as some other sort of fermented juice or extract serves as the main ingredient.<ref>Gibbons, E. Stalking the Wild Asparagus. David McKay, New York. 1962.</ref> It has also been used in a [[saison]] [[ale]] called Pissenlit (the French word for dandelion, literally meaning "wet the bed") made by [[Brasserie Fantôme]] in [[Belgium]]. [[Dandelion and burdock]] is a soft drink that has long been popular in the United Kingdom.

Another recipe using the plant is dandelion flower jam. In [[Silesia]] and other parts of Poland and the world, dandelion flowers are used to make a honey substitute [[syrup]] with added lemon (so-called ''May-honey''). Ground roasted dandelion root can be used as a non-caffeinated [[dandelion coffee|coffee substitute]].<ref name="Sztabowa-1990" />

===Diuretic===
The [[diuretic]] properties of ''T. officinale'', believed to be a result of the plant's high [[potassium]] content,<ref>{{Citation |last=Dog |first=Tieraona Low |chapter=CHAPTER 18 - Urinary Tract Infection |date=2005-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780443066399500265 |title=Women's Health in Complementary and Integrative Medicine |pages=293–306 |editor-last=Dog |editor-first=Tieraona Low |place=Saint Louis |publisher=Churchill Livingstone |language=en |isbn=978-0-443-06639-9 |access-date=2022-09-14}}</ref> have been well described. The leaves of the common dandelion have been used as a diuretic in [[traditional Chinese medicine]] for approximately 2,000 years, with other regions of the world using the plant in the same way; in French, a common name for ''T. officinale'' is ''pissenlit'', 'a colourful description of its diuretic activity'. A study conducted in 2009 noted 'promising' results regarding these diuretic properties, but that further studies would need to be conducted into the plant's efficacy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clare|first1=Bevin A.|last2=Conroy|first2=Richard S.|last3=Spelman|first3=Kevin|date=August 2009|title=The Diuretic Effect in Human Subjects of an Extract of Taraxacum officinale Folium over a Single Day|journal=Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine|volume=15|issue=8|pages=929–934|doi=10.1089/acm.2008.0152|issn=1075-5535|pmc=3155102|pmid=19678785}}</ref>

===Herbal medicine===
Dandelion has been used in [[traditional medicine]] in Europe, North America, and China.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Katrin Schütz, Reinhold Carle |author2=Andreas Schieber |name-list-style=amp |year=2006 |title=''Taraxacum''—a review on its phytochemical and pharmacological profile |journal=[[Journal of Ethnopharmacology]] |volume=107 |issue=3 |pages=313–323 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2006.07.021 |pmid=16950583 |bibcode=2006JEthn.107..313S }}</ref>

===Research===
Since asexually-reproducing dandelions produce genetically identical offspring, they are often useful as subjects for scientific research. For example, dandelions are used in studies where genetic differences between subjects needs to be minimal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=Keith L. |title=Dandelions 'remember' stress: heritable stress-induced methylation patterns in asexual dandelions |journal=The New Phytologist |date=2010 |volume=185 |issue=4 |pages=867–868 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.2010.03189.x |pmid=20356338 |bibcode=2010NewPh.185..867A }}</ref>

===Education===
Because of its worldwide distribution, familiarity, and presence in a wide variety of [[Folklore|folkloric]] traditions, the dandelion has been highlighted as a valuable tool for educators seeking to help children of varying cultural and ethnic backgrounds connect to science through [[ethnobotany]].<ref name="Esprivalo-2001">{{cite journal |last1=Esprivalo |first1=Pamela Sue |last2=Forney |first2=Scott |title=Cultivating Cultural Appreciation: ADDRESSING DIVERSITY THROUGH ETHNOBOTANY |journal=The Science Teacher |date=2001 |volume=68 |issue=3}}</ref>

===Folklore===
[[File:Hanna B. Senior Pics - 52344833092.jpg|thumb|upright|A [[woman]] blowing on the seed head of a dandelion]]
In [[folklore]], blowing on the seed head of a dandelion is used as a method of [[divination]] to tell [[fate]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/faustinafantasia00cowa/page/2/mode/2up|title=Faustina: a fantasia of autumn in the heart of Appalachia|author=[[Frank Cowan]]|year=1888|page=2|quote=As, when a child, divining, I have held Before my eyes a dandelion’s globe Of winged seeds, and blown against it ; till, Exhausted, lo ! in the persistent seeds, Or odd or even in my careful count, I found forthwith the fingering of Fate!}}</ref>

===Other===
Yellow dyes can be obtained from the flowers but little colour can be obtained from the roots of the plant.<ref name="Dyer-1976" /> The latex can be used as a kind of glue.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Complete Guide to Edible Wild Plants |publisher=[[Skyhorse Publishing]] |author=((United States Department of the Army)) |author-link=United States Department of the Army |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-60239-692-0 |location=New York |page=49 |language=en-US |oclc=277203364}}</ref>

==In culture==
Cultures worldwide tell stories about the dandelion and have culinary and medicinal uses for it. A Native American folktale tells the story of a golden haired girl who attracted the fancy of the South Wind. The South Wind was too lazy to pursue her, until one day he realised she had grown old and her hair had turned white. Supposedly, when the South Wind sighs over the loss of his chance to pursue the golden-haired girl, his breath sends the white-haired dandelion seeds scattering to propagate more golden-haired daughters.<ref name="Esprivalo-2001"/>
